extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and competition-level mathematics students studying abstract algebra and point-set topology
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and examples about metric-space properties (boundedness, completeness, total boundedness, compactness) and basic topology (open/closed, continuity, Hausdorff, connectedness, paths, homotopy, bases). Useful as a reference for solving exercises and understanding which properties are preserved under homeomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness (Definition 6.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space M is bounded if there is a constant D such that d(p, q) ≤ D for all p, q ∈ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulation (Proposition 6.1.2): for every point p ∈ M there is a radius R (possibly depending on p) with d(p,q) ≤ R for all q ∈ M. Examples: finite intervals like [0,1] and unit square are bounded; R^n and N are not. Exercise: use triangle inequality to show equivalence of diameter/radius formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totally bounded (Definition 6.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space is totally bounded if for any ε > 0, we can cover M with finitely many ε-neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications and examples: totally bounded ⇒ bounded (Exercise 6.1.6). In Euclidean space, bounded ⇔ totally bounded for subsets of R^n (Example 6.1.7(a)). Infinite discrete spaces are bounded but not totally bounded (Example 6.1.7(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy sequence (Definition 6.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence x1, x2, ... in metric space M is Cauchy if for any ε > 0, d(xm, xn) < ε for all sufficiently large m,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergent sequences are Cauchy (Question 6.2.2). Use this to define completeness. Example: rational approximations 1,1.4,1.41,... are Cauchy in Q but fail to converge in Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness (Definition 6.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space M is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges (to a point within M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R, closed interval [0,1], R^n, discrete spaces (trivially). Non-examples: Q and (0,1). Theorem 6.2.6: every metric space has a completion (completion construction). Example 6.2.7: Q completes to R. Remarks: completeness is a metric property, not topological (Remark 7.2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspace as metric space (Definition 6.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every subset S ⊆ M of a metric space inherits a metric by restricting the distance function; S is then a subspace of M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish absolute adjectives (e.g., 'complete', 'bounded') which apply to spaces and subspaces, from relative adjectives (e.g., 'open in M', 'closed in M') which depend on the ambient space. Exercise 6.4.2: in a complete metric space M, S ⊆ M is complete iff S is closed in M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric properties versus topological properties (Remark 7.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Complete' and '(totally) bounded' are metric properties and are not preserved under homeomorphism (i.e., they rely on the metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 6.3.1: (0,1) and R are homeomorphic but have different metric properties (one is totally bounded but not complete; the other is complete but not bounded). Thus these notions cannot be defined purely in terms of open sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity via preimage of open sets (Definition 7.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : X → Y of topological spaces is continuous at p if the preimage of every open neighborhood of f(p) contains an open neighborhood of p; f is continuous if it is continuous at every point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent characterization in metric spaces: preimage of every open set is open (Theorem 2.6.11 referenced). Exercise 7.2.6: a function is continuous iff the preimage of every closed set is closed. Homeomorphisms are bijections continuous in both directions and preserve topological properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeomorphism (Definition 7.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A homeomorphism between (X,τX) and (Y,τY) is a bijection inducing a bijection between τX and τY (i.e., it preserves open sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to the function and its inverse both being continuous (Question 7.2.3). Any property defined only in terms of open sets (a 'topological property') is preserved by homeomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hausdorff / T2 (Definition 7.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space X is Hausdorff if for any two distinct points p and q there exist disjoint open neighborhoods U and V with U ∩ V = ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All metric spaces are Hausdorff (Question 7.3.2). Hausdorff is a common separation axiom; many later results assume it. Used in Definition of 'compact' below (quasicompact + Hausdorff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and closed sets; closure (Definition 7.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a topological space X, S ⊆ X is closed if X \ S is open; the closure S̄ is the smallest closed set containing S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite intersections of closed sets are closed; unions of finitely many closed sets are closed (Question 7.2.5). Continuity can be rephrased using closed sets (Exercise 7.2.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connectedness and clopen sets (Definition 7.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset S of X is clopen if it is both closed and open. X is disconnected if it has a nontrivial clopen set; connected otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent: X is disconnected iff X can be written as a disjoint union of two nonempty open sets (Question 7.5.2). Examples: [0,1]∪[2,3] disconnected; [0,1] connected (Example 7.5.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Path and path-connectedness (Definitions 7.6.1 & 7.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A path in X is a continuous function γ : [0,1] → X. X is path-connected if every two points can be joined by some path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Path-connected ⇒ connected (Exercise 7.6.4). Examples: R^2 and S^1 are path-connected (Example 7.6.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homotopy of paths and simply connected (Definitions 7.7.1 & 7.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two paths with the same endpoints are path-homotopic if there exists a continuous deformation F : [0,1]^2 → X connecting them while fixing endpoints. A space is simply connected if it is path-connected and any two paths between the same endpoints are homotopic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivating examples: C is simply connected, C \ {0} is not (meteor analogy). Questions about what goes wrong when a point is removed (Question 7.7.3). R^n is simply connected for n ≥ 2 (Question 7.7.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for a topology (Definition 7.8.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A basis B for X is a collection of open sets such that every open set in X is a union of elements of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: open intervals form a basis for R. The r-neighborhoods form a basis for any metric space (Theorem 7.8.4). Use bases to generate and reason about open sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness (Definition 8.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric space M is sequentially compact if every sequence has a subsequence which converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-examples: R, (0,1), and non-complete or unbounded spaces (Example 8.1.3). Finite sets are compact (Question 8.1.4). Closed subsets of sequentially compact sets are compact (Proposition 8.1.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness via open covers (Definitions 8.3.1 & 8.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: An open cover is a collection {Uα} of open sets with ⋃ Uα = X. A space is quasicompact if every open cover has a finite subcover. A space is compact if it is quasicompact and Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric spaces are Hausdorff, so quasicompactness suffices there. Example: finite subcover illustration for unit square (Example 8.3.4). Open-cover definition is preferred for topological invariance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: sequentially compact ⇔ compact in metric spaces (Theorem 8.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For metric spaces, sequential compactness is equivalent to compactness (in the open-cover sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies using the open-cover definition for general topological spaces. Proof deferred in text; used to relate sequence-based intuition to topological definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano–Weierstraß / compact in R^n (Theorem 8.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of R^n is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Tychonoff to handle boxes and closed-subset argument. Caveat: 'closed and bounded' characterization is specific to R^n and fails in general metric spaces (Example 8.2.5: infinite discrete bounded closed set not compact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tychonoff product theorem for compactness (Theorem 8.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are compact spaces, then X × Y is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs like Bolzano–Weierstraß (product of compact intervals). Proof deferred or referenced to exercises (Problem 8E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and non-examples as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly supplies prototypical examples and non-examples for each notion (e.g., [0,1] bounded & compact, R^n not bounded, Q not complete, (0,1) not compact, infinite discrete space bounded but not totally bounded or compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples serve as anti-patterns and sanity checks when applying definitions; consult them when testing conjectures or constructing counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected algebra/ring problem statements (Problem 5B–5I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several algebraic facts/problems are listed: (5B) homomorphisms from fields are injective; (5C) pre-image of prime ideals under ring homomorphism is prime; (5D) finite integral domain ⇒ field; (5E) Krull's theorem: proper ideal J is contained in a maximal ideal in Noetherian rings (and via Zorn's lemma in general); (5F–5I) various classification/counting problems about prime/maximal ideals and ideals in localizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are stated as problems/theorems to be proved; include as important algebraic criteria/theorems relevant to the preceding chapter on rings. Notes: 5B includes remark that ring homomorphism cannot be zero since ψ(1_K)=1_R.
